name: Desia
confidence_why: Mahapatra (1985), the only work that describes Desia stress at all, calls it both predictable and phonemic, gives minimal pairs, and marks it on the first, second or final syllable in different examples, while Datta (2002) and the other works read say nothing about stress, so no placement or type can be stated.

catalog_quote: 3·4. Stress—/'/ Stress has phonemic value on a very limited number of words in Desia as it is a predictable phoneme in this dialect. All monosyllabic utterances carry the highest degree of stress. In words of more than three syllables there is always secondary stress on some subsequent syllables and usually it falls on that syllable which is farthest from the primarily stressed syllable. ... Stress is more distinctive in utterances with consonant/sonant/clusters in the first or second syllable. e.g./' tənḍ'/mouth, /as'ti/property,/kənḍe' k/a bit. [p. 33, sec. 4.4] As regards prominence, it is observed that (i) in disyllabic words when vowels are of same quality in both the syllables the first appears prominent, e.g. /,au/ 'vapour', but in a closed syllable the second syllable becomes prominent, e.g. /ələs/ 'lazy', (ii) in trisyllabics the order of prominence is 3 1 2, e.g. /tumeli/ 'hornet'. [p. 39, sec. 11] Final vowel—Final /ə/ is seldom retained on account of stress on initial syllable. jərə—jər (fever), kakərə—kakər (cold) [p. 15, sec. 0.3.7 Stress contrast:] 'pala/seedling pala'/go away 'duar/door du'ar/you carry 'kəla/soot kə'la/he did 'sapa/clean sapa'/whole lot

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 308 pp; IA item adibasi-1985-vol-25-issue-1-4, open). Locators hold: p. 37 = printed p. 29 (sec. 3.4 'Stress'), p. 23 = printed p. 15 (sec. 0.3.7 'Stress contrast'), p. 47 = printed p. 39 (sec. 11 'Loss of Vowel'). One locator error in the report: sec. 3.2 'Length' is printed p. 28 = p. 36, not 'p. 38' (p. 46 = printed 38 is the Appendix 'Loss of consonants'). The quotation was checked again: read from the page scan, not the scanned, which is garbage on this page. the prose of 3.4 is verbatim as quoted ('Stress has phonemic value on a very limited number of words in Desia as it is a predictable phoneme in this dialect. All monosyllabic utterances carry the highest degree of stress. In words…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source calls stress predictable (phonemic only in a handful of words) but never states the primary-stress position outright. The one explicit positional remark says final /ə/ is lost 'on account of stress on initial syllable', and the noun members of the minimal pairs carry initial stress ('pala 'seedling', 'duar 'door', 'kəla 'soot', 'sapa 'clean') while the verb-form members carry final/non-initial stress (pala' 'go away', du'ar 'you carry', kə'la 'he did', sapa' 'whole lot'). The examples in 3.4 itself, read with the stress mark preceding the stressed syllable, show second-syllable stress (kə'rat, se'tuwali, a'dar, as'ti), which conflicts with the initial-stress remark unless the mark is read as following the stressed syllable ('indicated by /'/ on the side', p. 11). Net: leaning toward default initial word stress with grammatically conditioned non-initial stress in verb forms, but the description is internally ambiguous.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'In words of more than three syllables there is always secondary stress on some subsequent syllables and usually it falls on that syllable which is farthest from the primarily stressed syllable' (p. 29).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is contrastive in 'a very limited number of words'; the contrast pairs (p. 15) oppose nouns with initial stress to verb forms with final stress; stress said to be 'more distinctive' when there is a consonant cluster in the first or second syllable; monosyllables carry the highest degree of stress. Phonetic (non-phonemic) vowel length falls 'in the penultimate position of a closed syllable and in the final position of a consonant cluster' (p. 38).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for 'utterances' and 'words' in citation-style examples (grammar based on the author's Koraput fieldwork); no phrase-level or instrumental data. The stress mark's placement convention is not fully consistent between p. 15 and p. 29, so the position reading should be reviewed against the page scan before cataloguing.
new_statements.identity_note: desi1235 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping node: Glottolog states Desiya [dso] and Adivasi Oriya [ort] 'simply divide the speakers of the same language along a state border' and points to adiv1239 (Kotia-Adivasi Oriya-Desiya). The source quoted (Mahapatra 1985) describes the Desia spoken in Koraput district, Odisha, i.e. exactly the [dso] side; the Andhra Pradesh side (Kotia/Adiwasi Oriya) was described separately by Gustafsson (SIL, 1974/1989), not examined here.

tone.quote: p. 28: "II. SUPRASEGMENTAL PHONEMES / 3. Description and Distribution / 3·1 Nasalization — Nasalization occurs with all the vowels. It is phonemic and can be treated as suprasegmental phoneme. … 3·2. Length— / Length or prolongation can be taken to be phonemic as it is contrastive. … 3·3. Juncture — Identical phonemic sequences meaning differently in different utterance medial positions prove the presence of a phonetic phenomena which can be identified as a suprasegmental phoneme of juncture." p. 29: "3·4. Stress—/'/ Stress has phonemic value on a very limited number of words in Desia as it is a predictable phoneme in this dialect. All monosyllabic utterances carry the highest degree of stress." p. 30: "III SYLLABLES" (no tone item in the suprasegmental section).
tone.locator: INDEX and Ch.1 Phonemics, II 'Suprasegmental Phonemes' secs 3.1-3.4, pp. 28-29; notation list 0.2 p. 14; clause intonation Ch.3 Syntax
tone.summary: The phonemic analysis posits no tone: the suprasegmental phonemes are nasalization, length, juncture and stress, and pitch figures only as the clause intonation contour; no explicit sentence on tone.
tone.says: The phonemic analysis posits no tone: the suprasegmental phonemes are nasalization, length, juncture and stress, and pitch figures only as the clause intonation contour; no explicit sentence on tone.
